subject: Mathematics
hook: What a maths report tells you, and what it hides.
body:
A maths report is an average of averages.

62 percent might be strong algebra and collapsed geometry, or steady mediocrity across everything. Those need opposite responses, and the number cannot tell them apart.

Ask for the question-level breakdown. Most schools have it and rarely send it unprompted.

That one request changes the whole conversation.
slides: What a maths report tells you, and what it hides.
A percentage is an average of averages
'Could apply himself' usually means one topic
Effort grades measure compliance, not learning
Ask for the question-level breakdown
Save this before the next report evening.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: Nobody is confident the first time.
body:
Nobody is confident the first time.

Shyness sounds like a personality, which makes it sound permanent. Unrehearsed is a state, and states change.

The difference between a child who freezes and a child who presents is usually eight rehearsals nobody scheduled.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Nobody is confident the first time.
BEAT (4-12s): Shyness is a personality. Unrehearsed is a state.
BEAT (12-20s): One sounds permanent. The other takes four weeks.
BEAT (20-29s): Nobody is fluent the first time they speak in front of people.
BEAT (29-34s): They are fluent the ninth time.
BEAT (34-43s): The gap is not courage. It is practice nobody scheduled.
CTA (43-48s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Coding
hook: Nine finished tutorials is not learning to code.
body:
Nine finished tutorials is not learning to code.

Copying a tutorial line by line teaches typing. The learning happens when something breaks and a child has to work out why, and nothing in a finished tutorial ever breaks.

Ask what happens in week three when the code will not run.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Nine finished tutorials is not learning to code.
BEAT (4-9s): Copying a tutorial teaches typing.
BEAT (9-15s): The learning happens when it breaks.
BEAT (15-22s): And nothing in a finished tutorial ever breaks.
BEAT (22-31s): Ask what your child does in week three when the code fails.
BEAT (31-36s): That answer is the whole course.
CTA (36-41s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Mathematics
hook: The Year 9 decision most parents make by accident.
body:
The Year 9 decision most parents make by accident.

Set placement decides which tier your child is entered for, and the tier caps the grade available. That narrows what they can take at A Level, years before anyone mentions A Levels.

Most families find out on results day.

Ask which tier your child is on track for. Ask in Year 9, not Year 11.
slides: The Year 9 decision most parents make by accident.
Set placement in Year 9 shapes Year 12
Foundation tier caps the grade, quietly
Moving up is possible, but the evidence has to exist
The window is roughly eighteen months
Send this to a parent with a child in Year 9.

subject: Coding
hook: What to actually teach a child about AI.
body:
What to actually teach a child about AI.

Not prompting. Prompting will be obsolete in two years and it was never the hard part.

The durable skill is judgement: knowing when the answer is wrong, where it came from, and when the tool should stay closed. A child who can spot a confident wrong answer is more employable than one who can write a clever prompt.

That skill is just critical thinking with a new surface. Which is good news, because we already know how to teach it.
slides: What to actually teach a child about AI.
How to check whether an answer is true
Where the answer came from
What it is confidently wrong about
When not to use it at all
Save this for the next homework argument.

subject: French
hook: Why your child can pass French and still not speak it.
body:
Why a child can score well in French and still freeze in Paris.

Written exams reward recall. Speaking requires retrieval under time pressure, which is a different skill using a different part of the memory, and almost nothing in a school term practises it.

A vocabulary list learned on Sunday and tested on Friday is stored, not owned.

Ask when your child last had to answer a question in French without knowing it was coming.
slides: Why your child can pass French and still not speak it.
Written exams reward recall, not retrieval
Vocabulary lists are stored, never used
Grammar is taught before anything is said
Nobody has ever had to answer quickly
Ask when your child last spoke French unscripted.

subject: General
hook: Ask when they decided they were bad at it.
body:
Ask when they decided they were bad at it.

Almost every 'I'm not a maths person' traces to a specific moment. The belief outlives the incident by a decade.

Things you can date are things you can undo.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Ask when they decided they were bad at it.
BEAT (4-11s): 'I'm not a maths person' is not an assessment.
BEAT (11-16s): It is a memory.
BEAT (16-23s): Usually one topic, one question, one afternoon.
BEAT (23-30s): The belief outlives the incident by ten years.
BEAT (30-37s): Things you can date are things you can undo.
CTA (37-42s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Science
hook: Four science questions that reveal whether a child understands.
body:
Four questions that reveal whether a child understands science or has memorised it.

None of them ask for a definition. A definition can be recited by a child who has understood nothing, which is why exams stopped rewarding them.

These four ask what the idea is connected to. Understanding is a shape, not a fact, and you can only see the shape from the edges.

Try one tonight over dinner. Two minutes, no marking, and you will know more than the last report told you.
slides: Four science questions that reveal whether a child understands.
What would change if this were not true?
Where have you seen this outside the book?
What is this a special case of?
What would you measure to test it?
Try one tonight. It takes two minutes.

subject: Mathematics
hook: The five-minute check that finds the gap.
body:
Five minutes, and no marking.

Give your child a question they already got right, and ask why the method works. Fluency without understanding shows up in seconds, and it is the best early warning there is.

Then set one from two years earlier. Watch where they pause, not what they answer.

The hesitation is the diagnosis.
slides: The five-minute check that finds the gap.
Ask them to explain, not to solve
Go back two years, not two weeks
Watch where they stop, not what they answer
Do it without a grade attached
Try this tonight.

subject: Coding
hook: Getting stuck is the subject.
body:
Getting stuck is the subject, not an interruption to it.

Every professional developer spends most of the day with something not working. A child who thinks being stuck means being bad at it quits around week three.

Say it out loud early.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Getting stuck is the subject.
BEAT (4-13s): Every developer spends most of the day with something broken.
BEAT (13-19s): That is not failing. That is the job.
BEAT (19-28s): A child who thinks stuck means bad will quit in week three.
BEAT (28-33s): Say it out loud early.
BEAT (33-38s): This is meant to be hard.
CTA (38-43s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: What to say the night before they present.
body:
What to say the night before your child presents.

'Just be confident' asks them to produce a feeling on demand, which nobody can do. It reads as pressure, not support.

What works is specific and physical. Name the part they know best, so they have somewhere solid to start. Tell them nobody can see nerves, because it is true and they assume otherwise. And tell them to go slower than feels right, because speed is what nerves do to a voice and slowing down is the only lever they can actually pull mid-sentence.
slides: What to say the night before they present.
'You know this bit best' - name the bit
'Nobody can tell you are nervous'
'Slow is the only trick that works'
Not: 'just be confident'
Save this for the next one.

subject: Coding
hook: Your child used AI for their homework. Now what?
body:
Your child used AI for their homework. The ban does not work.

It only moves the behaviour somewhere you cannot see, and removes your ability to teach anything about it.

What works is asking them to explain the work without the screen. The gap shows up in about ninety seconds, and it shows up to them, not just to you. That is a far better lesson than a rule.

Then agree what the tool is allowed to do next time. Explain a concept, yes. Write the paragraph, no. Children keep rules they helped write.
slides: Your child used AI for their homework. Now what?
Ask them to explain it without the screen
Find the one sentence they cannot defend
Agree what it is allowed to do next time
Do not ban it. It will just go underground
Save this before the argument.

subject: General
hook: Four questions before you pay a tutor anything.
body:
Four questions before you pay a tutor anything.

The first one does most of the work. If the answer is 'start the syllabus', walk away - it assumes the problem is coverage, and it almost never is.

A good tutor names a measure before they begin. 'More confident' is not a measure. 'She will close negative numbers in three weeks' is.

And listen carefully to the third answer. Explaining again, louder, is not teaching. Going backwards to find the missing step is.
slides: Four questions before you pay a tutor anything.
What will you do in the first session?
How will I know it is working?
What happens when she gets stuck?
Who else have you taught at this level?
Ask these before the first invoice.

subject: Mathematics
hook: Three months of revision. No movement.
body:
Three months of revision, no movement.

Working hard on the wrong topic is still working hard. It is just the most expensive kind, because the child pays in confidence and gets nothing back.

Find the gap first. Then the hours count.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Three months of revision. No movement.
BEAT (4-13s): Working hard on the wrong topic is still working hard.
BEAT (13-18s): It is just the most expensive kind.
BEAT (18-26s): The child pays in confidence and sees nothing back.
BEAT (26-31s): And concludes they are the problem.
BEAT (31-36s): They are not. The sequence is.
CTA (36-41s): Follow for the rest.

subject: French
hook: Examiners are not counting your words.
body:
Examiners are not counting your words.

They are checking tense control, justified opinions, and whether you can keep going when a word will not come.

Every candidate loses a word mid-sentence. The mark difference is whether they stop dead or say it another way.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Examiners are not counting your words.
BEAT (4-9s): They are checking three things.
BEAT (9-16s): Can you hold a tense across a whole answer.
BEAT (16-22s): Can you give an opinion and justify it.
BEAT (22-29s): Can you keep going when a word will not come.
BEAT (29-37s): Everyone loses a word. The mark is in the recovery.
CTA (37-42s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: How to fix a child who rushes when nervous.
body:
Nerves do not make a child quiet. They make a child fast.

And speed is the thing that costs marks, because nobody can follow it and the speaker cannot hear themselves think.

Telling them to slow down does not work under pressure. Marking the pauses on the page does, because it turns a feeling into an instruction.

The first line matters most. Rehearse it until it is automatic, and the rest arrives on a body that has already started.
slides: How to fix a child who rushes when nervous.
Mark the pauses on the page, physically
Rehearse the first line until it is automatic
Give them one thing to do with their hands
Record it once. They will hear it themselves
Try this before the next presentation.

subject: General
hook: The first session should not be chapter one.
body:
The first session should be diagnosis, not chapter one.

Nobody can teach a gap they have not located. Starting the syllabus on day one assumes the problem is coverage, and it almost never is.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): The first session should not be chapter one.
BEAT (4-13s): Starting the syllabus assumes the problem is coverage.
BEAT (13-18s): It almost never is.
BEAT (18-25s): It is one unfinished topic, somewhere behind.
BEAT (25-32s): Nobody can teach a gap they have not located.
BEAT (32-37s): Ask what happens in the first hour.
CTA (37-42s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Coding
hook: How to tell a real coding class from an expensive one.
body:
How to tell a real coding class from an expensive one.

Ask to see a student project from week eight, not the showreel. Week eight is where the difference lives: either everyone's project looks identical, which means they copied, or they look different, which means they built.

Ask what happens when a child finishes early. In a good class, they extend it. In a weak one, they wait.

And ask how many students share a screen. Two is fine, and often better. Four means three are watching.
slides: How to tell a real coding class from an expensive one.
Ask to see a student project from week eight
Ask what happens when someone finishes early
Ask how many students share one screen
Ask what they build that was not on the plan
Ask these before you enrol.

subject: Mathematics
hook: The two topics everything else is built on.
body:
Two topics carry almost everything after them.

Fractions in Year 7. Negative numbers in Year 8. Ratio, algebra, trigonometry and calculus all sit on top of them, and neither gets formally revisited once the class has moved on.

So a shaky Year 7 becomes a difficult Year 11, and it looks like the student got worse. They did not. The foundation was always thin and the building got taller.

It is not ability. It is sequence, and sequence problems have solutions.
slides: The two topics everything else is built on.
Fractions, around Year 7
Negative numbers, around Year 8
Ratio, algebra and trigonometry inherit both
Neither is ever formally revisited
Check these two before anything else.

subject: Coding
hook: Should my child still learn maths if AI can do it?
body:
Should my child still learn maths if AI can do it?

Yes, and more urgently than before. The skill now is telling when the answer is wrong, and that is subject knowledge, not technology.

You cannot audit an answer in a subject you do not understand.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Should my child still learn maths if AI can do it?
BEAT (4-9s): Yes. More urgently than before.
BEAT (9-17s): The skill now is telling when the answer is wrong.
BEAT (17-25s): That is not a tech skill. It is subject knowledge.
BEAT (25-34s): You cannot audit an answer in a subject you do not understand.
BEAT (34-41s): The tool raises the value of knowing things.
CTA (41-46s): Follow for the rest.

subject: General
hook: Three questions the brochure will not answer.
body:
Three questions for a school tour the brochure will not answer.

The third matters most. A school that puts its strongest teacher with students who are struggling believes ability can move. One that gives the bottom set to whoever is free has already decided it cannot.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Three questions the brochure will not answer.
BEAT (4-10s): What happens when a student falls behind?
BEAT (10-16s): How many dropped this subject last year?
BEAT (16-21s): Who teaches the bottom set?
BEAT (21-30s): That last one tells you what the school believes about ability.
BEAT (30-39s): You will learn more from it than the whole prospectus.
CTA (39-44s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: Four moments speaking decides the outcome.
body:
Speaking is the only school subject that is also every subsequent interview.

And almost nobody trains for it, because it does not appear on a report card. It appears at nineteen, in a room, when the grades have already done their job and something else is being assessed.

The useful thing about it is that it responds to practice faster than almost anything else on a timetable. Four weeks of deliberate work changes how a child sounds. Four weeks of maths rarely changes a grade.

Start earlier than feels necessary.
slides: Four moments speaking decides the outcome.
The university interview
The group project nobody wants to present
The first job interview, at nineteen
Every viva, defence and presentation after
Start earlier than feels necessary.

subject: French
hook: The revision that feels best works worst.
body:
The revision that feels best works worst.

Re-reading a vocabulary list is comfortable, so nothing is being strengthened. Covering it and writing it from memory feels worse and works.

Memory grows at the point of effortful recall.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): The revision that feels best works worst.
BEAT (4-11s): Re-reading the list is fluent and comfortable.
BEAT (11-18s): Nothing is hard, so nothing is strengthened.
BEAT (18-26s): Cover it. Write it from memory. That feels worse.
BEAT (26-33s): Memory grows at the point of effortful recall.
BEAT (33-38s): Not at the point of recognition.
CTA (38-43s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Mathematics
hook: What to say when they get a bad mark.
body:
What to say when the mark comes back low.

'Did you revise?' is a trial, and children defend themselves in trials rather than think. You will get a defence, not information.

Every question in this list points at the paper instead of the child, which is where the useful information is. 'Was it the topic or the timing' in particular separates two completely different problems that produce identical marks.

And 'show me the one you nearly got' is the fastest route back to a child who has stopped talking about it.
slides: What to say when they get a bad mark.
'Which question would you like to understand?'
'Was it the topic or the timing?'
'Show me the one you nearly got'
Not: 'did you revise?'
Save this for results week.

subject: Science
hook: Why practicals matter more than the mark suggests.
body:
Practicals carry more weight than their share of the marks suggests.

Method questions appear across every paper, and they are answered well by students who have actually stood over an experiment that did not work. You can revise a method. You cannot revise the instinct for what usually goes wrong.

There is a second reason. Ten years later, the mole calculations are gone and the afternoon the reaction turned an unexpected colour is still there.

A subject people remember is a subject people carry on with.
slides: Why practicals matter more than the mark suggests.
They are where the theory becomes falsifiable
Method questions carry marks in every paper
'What went wrong' is examinable, and teachable
It is the only part students remember in ten years
Ask what they did in the lab this term.

subject: Coding
hook: Build one thing someone else uses.
body:
Every child should build one thing other people actually use.

The shift happens the first time someone reports a bug. The work has consequences outside the classroom, and they stop asking whether it is finished and start asking whether it works.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Build one thing someone else uses.
BEAT (4-9s): Not a project marked by a teacher.
BEAT (9-17s): Something small and real, for one actual person.
BEAT (17-26s): The shift happens the first time someone reports a bug.
BEAT (26-33s): Now it has consequences outside the classroom.
BEAT (33-42s): They stop asking if it is finished. They ask if it works.
CTA (42-47s): Follow for the rest.

subject: General
hook: What a good session actually looks like.
body:
What a good session actually looks like from the outside.

The student talks more than the tutor. That single ratio separates teaching from lecturing, and it is easy to check - just ask your child who did most of the talking.

Something goes wrong on purpose, because a student who has only seen worked examples has never practised the actual skill, which is recovering.

And it ends with something they can do without help. Not something they watched. Something they can do.
slides: What a good session actually looks like.
The student talks more than the tutor
At least one thing goes wrong on purpose
It ends with something they can do alone
The next gap is already named
Ask what happened in the last session.

subject: General
hook: No child is behind.
body:
No child is behind. A topic was left unfinished, and everything after it inherited the gap.

That is not a kindness, it is a diagnosis. One version makes a fourteen year old the problem. The other makes it a sequence, and sequences can be reordered.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): No child is behind.
BEAT (4-9s): A topic was left unfinished.
BEAT (9-17s): Everything built on top of it inherited the gap.
BEAT (17-26s): 'Behind' describes the child and offers nothing to do.
BEAT (26-34s): 'Unfinished topic' tells you exactly where to go.
BEAT (34-42s): Same situation. Completely different next Monday.
CTA (42-47s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Mathematics
hook: Reading worked examples is not revision.
body:
Reading worked examples is not revision.

The answer is already on the page, so nothing is retrieved and nothing sticks. It gets filed under 'seen', which is not the same as 'can do'.

Close the book. Start the question. Being stuck is the part that teaches.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Reading worked examples is not revision.
BEAT (4-9s): The answer is already on the page.
BEAT (9-16s): Nothing is at risk, so nothing is learned.
BEAT (16-23s): The brain files it under 'seen', not 'can do'.
BEAT (23-32s): A blank page is uncomfortable for the reason it works.
BEAT (32-41s): One closed-book question beats an hour of highlighting.
CTA (41-46s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: What to say the night before a presentation.
body:
What to say the night before a presentation.

'You'll be fine' closes the conversation. It sounds like reassurance and lands like a door shutting, because the child still has the fear and now has nowhere to put it.

Name it instead. 'Most people go blank somewhere in the middle. What do you do if that happens?' turns a vague dread into one thing with a plan attached.

Then ask for the first line out loud, once. The opening is where the nerves live, and hearing it in a kitchen makes the classroom quieter.
slides: What to say the night before a presentation.
Ask them to say the first line out loud
Do not offer to rewrite it at 9pm
Name the fear instead of denying it
Agree what happens if they lose their place
Save this for the night before.

subject: Coding
hook: Six languages is not six times the learning.
body:
Six languages is not six times the learning.

Syntax is the cheapest part of programming and the easiest to look up. What transfers between languages is decomposition, naming, testing and reading an error properly.

One language, held long enough to finish something that runs, teaches every one of those.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Six languages is not six times the learning.
BEAT (4-11s): Syntax is the cheapest part of programming.
BEAT (11-19s): A reference page hands it to you in thirty seconds.
BEAT (19-27s): What transfers is breaking a problem into parts.
BEAT (27-35s): Naming things. Testing. Reading the error properly.
BEAT (35-44s): One language, held long enough to finish something, teaches all of it.
CTA (44-49s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Coding
hook: AI can draft the essay. It cannot defend it.
body:
AI can draft the essay. It cannot defend it.

The useful question at home is not whether a tool was used. It is whether your child could still hold the argument with the laptop shut.

That is trainable. A finished document does not train it.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): AI can draft the essay. It cannot defend it.
BEAT (4-11s): Unsupervised work is becoming weaker evidence.
BEAT (11-20s): Work produced in a room with a teacher is becoming stronger.
BEAT (20-29s): The spoken answer. The timed paper. The follow-up question.
BEAT (29-36s): So the question is not whether AI was used.
BEAT (36-45s): It is whether your child could hold the argument with the laptop shut.
CTA (45-50s): Follow for the rest.

subject: French
hook: Four reasons French vocabulary will not stick.
body:
Four reasons French vocabulary will not stick.

Most lists get learned French to English, because that is the direction the test runs. Then the speaking assessment asks for the opposite and the word is not there.

Words also arrive stripped of context. 'Chercher' on a list is a translation. 'Je cherche mes clés' is a memory, and memories survive longer than translations.

And almost none of it is said aloud, so the mouth has never made the sound under pressure.

Same twenty words. Both directions, in sentences, out loud, twice across a week. That is the whole change.
slides: Four reasons French vocabulary will not stick.
Word lists are learned in one direction only
Nothing is ever said out loud
The words arrive without a sentence around them
Revision happens once, the night before
Send this to a parent of a Year 9.

subject: Mathematics
hook: That sentence was meant as comfort.
body:
That sentence was meant as comfort.

Telling a child you were bad at maths sounds like solidarity and lands like a diagnosis. Nobody keeps pushing at something their own parent has called impossible for people like them.

Swap the identity for a timeline: that topic took a long time to click, and then it clicked.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): That sentence was meant as comfort.
BEAT (4-13s): Telling a child you were bad at maths lands as a diagnosis.
BEAT (13-19s): The intention is 'you are not alone'.
BEAT (19-26s): What arrives is 'this runs in the family'.
BEAT (26-33s): Children take inherited limits very seriously.
BEAT (33-42s): Try: that topic took a long time to click for a lot of people.
CTA (42-47s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Science
hook: Memorising the method gets almost none of the marks.
body:
Memorising the method gets almost none of the marks.

Practical questions ask why the control was there, what an anomalous reading means, and how the method could be improved. Those marks separate a middling script from a strong one.

A results table cannot teach any of them.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Memorising the method gets almost none of the marks.
BEAT (4-12s): Practical questions rarely stop at what happened.
BEAT (12-17s): Why was the control there?
BEAT (17-23s): What does the anomalous reading mean?
BEAT (23-28s): How would you improve the method?
BEAT (28-36s): None of that can be revised from a results table.
CTA (36-41s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Mathematics
hook: The fast child is not always the strong one.
body:
The fast child is not always the strong one.

Speed early usually means prior exposure, not capacity. The stall tends to come around Year 10, when the subject stops rewarding recall and starts asking for reasoning.

The child who works slowly and asks why has been building the part that lasts.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): The fast child is not always the strong one.
BEAT (4-13s): Speed in Year 7 usually means they met the topic before.
BEAT (13-18s): Real advantage. Temporary one.
BEAT (18-24s): Fast children often stall around Year 10.
BEAT (24-33s): Recall was rewarded. Then the subject asked for reasoning.
BEAT (33-42s): The careful child who asks why was building the durable thing.
CTA (42-47s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Coding
hook: What week one of a real coding course looks like.
body:
What week one of a real coding course looks like.

Something should run on the first day. Not a slide about what programming is, not an hour of theory about variables. Working code, on screen, that the student can point at.

And something should break on the first day, deliberately, while there is a teacher in the room. A child who has only ever seen code work has never practised the actual job.

Then the error message gets read out loud rather than scrolled past. Most beginners never learn that the computer already told them what was wrong.

By the end of week one, they should have changed the thing into something that was not in the plan.
slides: What week one of a real coding course looks like.
Something runs on day one
Something breaks on day one too
The error message gets read, not skipped
The student changes it into their own thing
Ask what week one looks like before you enrol.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: 'We build confidence' cannot be wrong. That is the problem.
body:
'We build confidence' cannot be wrong. That is the problem.

An answer that could never turn out to be false has not told you anything. 'Every student presents twice a term' can be checked. So can a rubric you are allowed to read.

Ask for the number, the frequency, or the document.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): 'We build confidence' cannot be wrong. That is the problem.
BEAT (4-10s): Nothing in that sentence can be verified.
BEAT (10-17s): 'Every student presents twice a term' can be.
BEAT (17-26s): So can the size of the debating society against the year group.
BEAT (26-35s): If an answer could not turn out to be false, it told you nothing.
BEAT (35-43s): Ask for the number, the frequency, or the document.
CTA (43-48s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Coding
hook: How to ask about the AI without starting a row.
body:
How to ask about the AI without starting a row.

'Did you use AI for this?' is an accusation with a yes-or-no exit, and both answers end the conversation.

'What did it get wrong?' does not. It assumes use, skips the confession, and lands straight on the only skill that matters: whether your child can spot a confident sentence that is untrue.

'What did you type to get that?' is the second good question. The prompt shows the thinking. A vague prompt means the tool did the work; a specific one means your child did.

And set the rule between deadlines. Nobody negotiates well at eleven at night.
slides: How to ask about the AI without starting a row.
Ask what it got wrong, not whether it was used
Ask them to explain one paragraph aloud
Ask what they typed to get it
Agree the line before the next deadline, not during
Save this before the next assignment.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: 'Make eye contact' is not an instruction.
body:
'Make eye contact' is not an instruction.

Without a method children sweep the room, land on nobody and look more nervous than when they started.

One face, one sentence. Finish the sentence, then move. Three or four faces in rotation. It paces the talk and it reads as calm.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): 'Make eye contact' is not an instruction.
BEAT (4-10s): It is like telling someone to be taller.
BEAT (10-17s): So they sweep the room and land on nobody.
BEAT (17-22s): The method: one face, one sentence.
BEAT (22-31s): Finish the sentence, then move. Three or four faces, in rotation.
BEAT (31-39s): It gives the eyes a job, so they stop searching.
CTA (39-44s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Mathematics
hook: A Level Maths does not start in Year 12.
body:
A Level Maths does not start in Year 12. It starts with algebraic fluency in Year 10.

The first term assumes rearranging, factorising, surds and indices are automatic, and moves at a pace that does not allow for relearning them. A student who can do that algebra slowly and carefully is, in that room, a student who cannot do it.

This is why strong IGCSE grades sometimes turn into a difficult October. The grade measured whether they could get there. A Level measures whether they can get there without thinking about it.

The fix belongs to the summer between, and it is narrow: fluency drills on the algebra they already know.
slides: A Level Maths does not start in Year 12.
It starts with algebraic fluency in Year 10
Rearranging is assumed, not taught again
Surds and indices arrive with no warm-up
The first term is the fastest term
Send this to a parent with a child in Year 11.

subject: French
hook: Good at French on paper, stuck out loud.
body:
Good at French on paper, stuck out loud.

Reading is recognition with time attached. Speaking is recall against a clock, choosing a verb ending live, in front of someone. A child can be strong in one and lost in the other.

Speaking practice has to be deliberate, because homework will never be it.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Good at French on paper, stuck out loud.
BEAT (4-11s): Reading is recognition, with time attached.
BEAT (11-19s): Speaking is recall against a clock, with an audience.
BEAT (19-27s): Different subjects that happen to share a vocabulary.
BEAT (27-36s): The reading mark hides the gap until the speaking assessment.
BEAT (36-45s): Homework is written because written can be marked in a pile.
CTA (45-50s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Science
hook: Combined or separate sciences: what actually changes.
body:
Combined or separate sciences: what actually changes.

Separate sciences are usually more content rather than harder content, and they cost a timetable slot that has to come from somewhere. Often that somewhere is a language or a humanity your child would have enjoyed.

The decision that matters is not prestige, it is what your child wants at A Level and what your specific sixth form asks for. Entry requirements differ between schools, so the only reliable answer comes from the school itself.

Ask that question directly, in Year 9, and take the answer in writing. It converts an anxious guess into a scheduling decision.
slides: Combined or separate sciences: what actually changes.
Separate sciences cover more content, not harder content
Three sciences means three slots on the timetable
Combined keeps a language or a humanity alive
Neither closes A Level Sciences by itself
Ask the school what their sixth form expects.

subject: Coding
hook: Red text is not a telling-off.
body:
Red text is not a telling-off.

The error message is the most specific piece of help available, and most beginners never read it. Eyes slide off, hands go up.

One habit fixes it: say the message out loud before touching the keyboard. Being stuck becomes a procedure instead of an emergency.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Red text is not a telling-off.
BEAT (4-11s): The instinct is to feel caught and look away.
BEAT (11-19s): The line number goes unread. The message goes unread.
BEAT (19-28s): But that message is the most specific help in the session.
BEAT (28-37s): Written by the machine, free, at the exact moment it is needed.
BEAT (37-46s): The habit: say it out loud before touching the keyboard.
CTA (46-51s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Mathematics
hook: The marks were lost in the working, not the answer.
body:
The marks were lost in the working, not the answer.

Method marks reward a visible process. A wrong final value with three correct written steps can outscore a bare answer that happened to be right.

Write the substitution. Write the rearrangement. It costs four seconds a question.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): The marks were lost in the working, not the answer.
BEAT (4-10s): Examiners mark a process, not a number.
BEAT (10-19s): Three visible correct steps can outscore a bare right answer.
BEAT (19-27s): Students who work in their heads lose this quietly.
BEAT (27-32s): Tidy books. Inexplicable marks.
BEAT (32-41s): Write the substitution. Write the rearrangement. Four seconds.
CTA (41-46s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Coding
hook: Same tool. One child gets weaker, one gets stronger.
body:
Same tool. One child gets weaker, one gets stronger.

The difference is the request. 'Answer this' hands over the thinking. 'Give three approaches, then compare them' keeps it, and keeps the child practising the part no tool supplies.

Banning it usually just moves it somewhere unsupervised.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Same tool. One child gets weaker, one gets stronger.
BEAT (4-11s): The difference is the shape of the request.
BEAT (11-17s): 'Answer this' hands over the thinking.
BEAT (17-25s): 'Give three approaches, then compare them' keeps it.
BEAT (25-34s): One learns the tool is smarter. One learns judgement is the product.
BEAT (34-39s): Ask for options, not answers.
CTA (39-44s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: A speaking assessment is not testing charisma.
body:
A speaking assessment is not testing charisma.

It tests structure: a position, two reasons, back to the position. Then whether that position survives a follow-up question, which is where most students fold.

Children who look naturally good at this are simply practised.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): A speaking assessment is not testing charisma.
BEAT (4-11s): Position, two reasons, back to the position.
BEAT (11-20s): That sounds prepared even when it is invented on the spot.
BEAT (20-27s): Then: does the position survive one follow-up?
BEAT (27-36s): That is where most students fold and agree with the examiner.
BEAT (36-44s): None of it is personality. All of it is a drill.
CTA (44-49s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Mathematics
hook: More practice will not fix a misunderstanding.
body:
More practice will not fix a misunderstanding.

Repetition makes a wrong method faster and harder to unlearn. A child getting the same kind of question wrong is not under-practised, she is confidently doing something that does not work.

Watch one question out loud. Find the step. Then practise.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): More practice will not fix a misunderstanding.
BEAT (4-10s): Practice makes a correct method faster.
BEAT (10-16s): It makes an incorrect method faster too.
BEAT (16-25s): And much harder to remove, because it has been rehearsed.
BEAT (25-32s): Watch one question being done out loud instead.
BEAT (32-40s): The broken step is usually visible in ninety seconds.
CTA (40-45s): Follow for the rest.

subject: French
hook: The Sunday hour is mostly recovery.
body:
The Sunday hour is mostly recovery.

Language memory fades daily, so a week-long gap means opening with twenty minutes of re-warming. Four ten-minute contacts keep the sound in the mouth.

Same total time. Different subject by half term.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): The Sunday hour is mostly recovery.
BEAT (4-12s): Language fades on a daily clock, not a weekly one.
BEAT (12-19s): So twenty minutes go on ground already covered.
BEAT (19-27s): Four short contacts keep the sound in the mouth.
BEAT (27-36s): Pronunciation is muscular. Muscles are not maintained weekly.
BEAT (36-45s): Ten minutes is small enough that nobody argues about it.
CTA (45-50s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Coding
hook: A coding club is not a coding course.
body:
A coding club is not a coding course.

A club is designed so a child who missed last week still enjoys this week. That constraint is exactly what makes progression impossible.

Ask what week eight assumes that week one taught. If nothing, it is exposure, not a course.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): A coding club is not a coding course.
BEAT (4-13s): A club is exposure, and that is worth having at eleven.
BEAT (13-22s): But a club is built so that missing a week costs nothing.
BEAT (22-29s): Which means the difficulty can never rise.
BEAT (29-35s): A course has an order and a next thing.
BEAT (35-43s): Ask what week eight assumes that week one taught.
CTA (43-48s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Science
hook: The wrong prediction is the useful one.
body:
The wrong prediction is the useful one.

When predictions get written after the results, the experiment stops being an experiment. Nothing can surprise anyone, and surprise is where the learning was.

A wrong prediction honestly recorded is better work than a right one copied off the board.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): The wrong prediction is the useful one.
BEAT (4-11s): Students learn to write the safe prediction.
BEAT (11-17s): Or to write it after the results arrive.
BEAT (17-24s): At that point nothing can surprise anyone.
BEAT (24-32s): And surprise is where the understanding was hiding.
BEAT (32-41s): What did the model get wrong? That is the whole subject.
CTA (41-46s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Mathematics
hook: Same grade. Completely different next year.
body:
Same grade. Completely different next year.

A grade built on remembered procedures and one built on understood procedures look identical on results day. They stop looking identical the first time a question arrives in an unfamiliar shape.

Ask why the method works. 'That's just how you do it' is the fragile answer.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Same grade. Completely different next year.
BEAT (4-13s): A grade can be built on remembered procedures or understood ones.
BEAT (13-20s): The paper often cannot tell the difference.
BEAT (20-27s): Then a question arrives in an unfamiliar shape.
BEAT (27-36s): One student adapts. One waits to be told which method this is.
BEAT (36-45s): Ask why the method works. The answer tells you which you have.
CTA (45-50s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Coding
hook: How AI actually gets used in a lesson.
body:
How AI actually gets used in a lesson.

To generate eight variations of the question that exposed the gap. To play the student a child has to teach. To produce a confident wrong answer worth arguing with.

Never to produce work that gets handed in. That inverts the point.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): How AI actually gets used in a lesson.
BEAT (4-13s): As a supply of practice: eight versions of one question type.
BEAT (13-19s): As a student the child has to teach.
BEAT (19-27s): The questions it asks back expose what they missed.
BEAT (27-35s): As an opponent, producing a confident wrong solution.
BEAT (35-42s): Never to produce work that gets handed in.
CTA (42-47s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Public Speaking
hook: The quiet child in class is often the loudest at home.
body:
The quiet child in class is often the loudest at home.

Not personality. Audience. The fluency is already there; what changed is the cost of being wrong in front of thirty peers.

One prepared sentence offered early in the lesson does more than a term of being told to speak up.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): The quiet child in class is often the loudest at home.
BEAT (4-11s): That is not personality. That is audience.
BEAT (11-16s): The fluency is already there.
BEAT (16-25s): What changed is the cost of being wrong in front of thirty peers.
BEAT (25-32s): So do not aim for brave. Aim for rehearsed.
BEAT (32-41s): One prepared sentence, offered early, beats a term of 'speak up'.
CTA (41-46s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Mathematics
hook: The Year 11 problem started in Year 7.
body:
The Year 11 problem started in Year 7.

Fractions get marked as done and then quietly underpin ratio, probability, rates and every algebraic fraction that follows. Marks lost across several unrelated topics are often one gap, four years upstream.

Ask for three-quarters divided by two-fifths tonight, with the reasoning out loud.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): The Year 11 problem started in Year 7.
BEAT (4-11s): Fractions arrive early and get marked as done.
BEAT (11-20s): Then they hold up ratio, probability, rates and rearranging.
BEAT (20-29s): The topic never leaves. It stops being called fractions.
BEAT (29-38s): Marks lost across unrelated topics are often one gap, upstream.
BEAT (38-43s): Nobody reteaches it after Year 8.
CTA (43-48s): Follow for the rest.

subject: French
hook: Do not correct the accent at the dinner table.
body:
Do not correct the accent at the dinner table.

A child speaking French at home is producing language with no script, in front of the audience that matters most. Interrupting to fix a vowel makes speaking riskier than silence.

Correction belongs in the lesson. Accuracy has a whole term to arrive.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Do not correct the accent at the dinner table.
BEAT (4-13s): A child speaking French at home is doing the hardest thing there is.
BEAT (13-22s): No script, in front of people whose opinion actually matters.
BEAT (22-31s): Fix a vowel and speaking now carries a risk silence does not.
BEAT (31-36s): So the sentence stops coming.
BEAT (36-45s): Correction belongs in the lesson. At home, keep it coming.
CTA (45-50s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Coding
hook: A ban is a position, not a policy.
body:
A ban is a position, not a policy.

Ask what is allowed, what must be declared, and how assessment has changed in response. The last one matters most, because it is the only answer that costs the school something.

Ask for the document. A school that has one will hand it over.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): A ban is a position, not a policy.
BEAT (4-10s): It says what the school disapproves of.
BEAT (10-18s): Not what happens to a piece of homework on a Tuesday.
BEAT (18-27s): A policy names what is allowed and what must be declared.
BEAT (27-34s): And how assessment has changed in response.
BEAT (34-43s): That last part is the only one that costs the school something.
CTA (43-48s): Follow for the rest.

subject: Coding
hook: Scratch is not a toy that gets outgrown.
body:
Scratch is not a toy that gets outgrown.

Loops, conditionals, variables and events are the same concepts a first computer science course teaches. Text adds syntax, and syntax is the cheap part.

Move across when the blocks become the slow part, not when the calendar says so.
reel_script:
HOOK (0-4s): Scratch is not a toy that gets outgrown.
BEAT (4-12s): Loops, conditionals, variables, events, sequence.
BEAT (12-19s): Those are first-year computer science concepts.
BEAT (19-28s): What text adds is syntax, and syntax is not the hard part.
BEAT (28-37s): Push a child out early and they fight semicolons instead of structure.
BEAT (37-45s): Move across when the blocks become the slow part.
CTA (45-50s): Follow for the rest.
